Alpöge’s counterexample to the JC, Economic Stabilization, and Zhao’s Vanishing Conjecture

Michiel de Bondt
Abstract

In this paper, we apply stabilization techniques which are economic in the number of added dimensions to a slightly tweaked version of Alpöge’s counterexample to JC⁡(3)\mathrm{JC}(3) and JC⁡(3,7)\mathrm{JC}(3,7). The first idea which lead to more economic stabilization is to bypass the degree 3 reduction of Bass, Connell and Wright in the construction of a counterexample to HJC⁡(n)\mathrm{HJC}(n). We construct counterexamples to HJC⁡(15)\mathrm{HJC}(15), VC⁡(28)\mathrm{VC}(28), and HVC⁡(30)\mathrm{HVC}(30). On the other hand, we will perform degree 3 reduction after all to obtain counterexamples of low degree. We construct counterexamples to JC⁡(12,3)\mathrm{JC}(12,3), HJC⁡(18,3)\mathrm{HJC}(18,3), VC⁡(34,4)\mathrm{VC}(34,4), and HVC⁡(36,4)\mathrm{HVC}(36,4). As an encore, we construct a cubic-linear counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension 90. All presented counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture (Vanishing Conjecture) are over the (Gaussian) integers.

1 Introduction

The Jacobian Conjecture, posed by Ott-Heinrich Keller in 1939, asserts that any polynomial map F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} with a nowhere-vanishing Jacobian determinant (det𝒥⁡(F)∈ℂ×\det\mathcal{J}(F)\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}) is globally invertible. We denote this classic conjecture in dimension nn as JC⁡(n)\mathrm{JC}(n), and restrict it to polynomial maps of exact degree dd as JC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{JC}(n,d). If the non-linear part of the mapping is strictly homogeneous of degree dd, the corresponding assertion is denoted as HJC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{HJC}(n,d).

For nearly nine decades, this problem stood as one of the most notorious challenges in algebraic geometry and polynomial algebra. In July 2026, Levent Alpöge published a historic breakthrough, constructing an explicit, non-injective polynomial counterexample establishing the falsity of JC⁡(3)\mathrm{JC}(3) and, more specifically, JC⁡(3,7)\mathrm{JC}(3,7) [1].

Alpöge’s counterexample immediately revitalized interest in several long-standing conjectures known to be stably-equivalent to the Jacobian Conjecture. Chief among these is the Zhao’s Vanishing Conjecture (for the Laplace operator), introduced by Wenhua Zhao in 2007 [10], which we will henceforth abbreviate as the Vanishing Conjecture. The conjecture states that for the standard Laplace operator Δ=∑∂2∂xk2\Delta=\sum\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial x_{k}^{2}} and a polynomial P∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2,…,xn]P\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}], if Δm​(Pm)=0\Delta^{m}(P^{m})=0 for all m≥1m\geq 1, then Δm​(Pm+1)=0\Delta^{m}(P^{m+1})=0 for all m≫0m\gg 0. We denote this assertion for polynomials in nn variables as VC⁡(n)\mathrm{VC}(n), and specify the restriction to polynomials of exact degree dd as VC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{VC}(n,d). When the underlying potential PP is strictly homogeneous (of degree dd), the conjecture is denoted as HVC⁡(n)\mathrm{HVC}(n) (HVC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{HVC}(n,d)). Zhao established that the universal (all-dimensional) Jacobian Conjecture is completely equivalent to the universal Vanishing Conjecture for (quartic) homogeneous polynomials under the standard Laplacian.

To systematically manipulate and stabilize these counterexamples, it is highly convenient to operate within the class of unipotent polynomial automorphisms. A polynomial map F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} is called a unipotent Jacobian map if it takes the form F=X+HF=X+H, where the Jacobian matrix 𝒥⁡(H)\mathcal{J}(H) is strictly nilpotent. We define UJC⁡(n)\mathrm{UJC}(n) as the statement that every unipotent Jacobian map over ℂ\mathbb{C} in dimension nn is globally invertible, and denote its restriction to exact degree dd as UJC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{UJC}(n,d). By standard algebraic frameworks, any counterexample to JC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{JC}(n,d) can be embedded into a higher-dimensional unipotent setting without altering its structural noninjectivity.

To transport a counterexample from the Jacobian framework to the vanishing arena, researchers traditionally rely on the classical Bass–Connell–Wright (BCW) reduction [2]. The BCW procedure introduces a vast sequence of auxiliary variables to systematically force the degree of any Keller map down to 3, and homogenizing the non-linear part. In this paper, we proceed differently: we skip the intermediate degree-3 reduction entirely and synchronize the system by making the non-linear part homogeneous immediately, without altering the natural highest degree of the counterexample. As detailed in Section 2, this direct, single-step homogenization preserves tight control over the variable expansion, terminating at an exact total dimension of:

M=n+∑i=1nmax⁡(deg⁡(Fi)−2, 0)+1=𝒪⁡(n⋅d)M=n+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\max(\deg(F_{i})-2,\,0)+1=\mathcal{O}(n\cdot d) (1)

where d=maxi⁡(deg⁡Fi)d=\max_{i}(\deg F_{i}) represents the maximum degree of the system. Applied to our volume-normalized version of Alpöge’s mapping, this stabilization strategy yields explicit counterexamples to UJC⁡(14)\mathrm{UJC}(14), UJC⁡(14,7)\mathrm{UJC}(14,7), HJC⁡(15)\mathrm{HJC}(15), and HJC⁡(15,7)\mathrm{HJC}(15,7).

In contrast, forcing a degree-3 restriction does not possess such a direct, predictable complexity bound. Because the traditional BCW method requires splitting higher-degree components into extensive binary trees of lower-degree cofactors, the stable configuration space is widely expected to suffer from extreme dimensional inflation. Indeed, in a recent preprint by Long [6], in which the immediate aftermath of Alpöge’s breakthrough is explored, a direct application of the cubic–homogeneous BCW reduction is performed without any optimization of the dimension outcome, leading to a stable homogeneous map in dimension 79. Based on these initial results, one might easily conclude that any degree-3 BCW reduction is inherently expensive and dimensionally prohibitive.

Heuristically, this assumption can be heavily nuanced by employing dimensionally economic stabilization techniques. As detailed in Section 4, by abandoning dynamic variable generation in favor of a fixed, pre-optimized initial grid and deploying a two-tier quotient sweeping phase based on the quadratic anchors x1​x2x_{1}x_{2} and x1​x3x_{1}x_{3}, the algebraic overhead can be radically compressed. Through a careful term-by-term puzzle, the cubic–homogeneous reduction terminates at only 21 dimensions, built over a 14-dimensional cubic base map. This allows us to construct explicit low-degree counterexamples to JC⁡(14,3)\mathrm{JC}(14,3), UJC⁡(20,3)\mathrm{UJC}(20,3), and HJC⁡(21,3)\mathrm{HJC}(21,3), revealing a surprising structural efficiency within the stabilized coordinate rings of the counterexample.

The dimensions 1414 and 2121 respectively seem astonishing compared to the corresponding numbers 3939 and 7979 by Long. But the impressiveness of these numbers vanished when I found out that Roy van Rijn had come to dimensions 1212 and 1919. Without studying Roy van Rijn’s construction, I tried to improve my own construction. Because of Eq. (1), I knew that Roy van Rijn’s 1212-dimensional construction had exactly 19−12−1=619-12-1=6 cubic components, just as my 1414-dimensional construction (21−14−1=621-14-1=6). So I tried to find a 1212-dimensional cubic construction with 66 cubic components, and I found one. It appeared to be essentially the same as Roy van Rijn’s construction. A day later, I tried to find a 1212-dimensional cubic construction with only 55 cubic components, since that would reduce to a cubic homogeneous construction in dimension 12+5+1=1812+5+1=18, and again, I found one. These constructions are also described in Section 4. It appeared that my last construction can by applied partially, to obtain counterexamples to JC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{JC}(n,d), UJC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{UJC}(n,d) and HJC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{HJC}(n,d) for d=4,5,6d=4,5,6.

The Hessian Conjecture asserts that any Hessian-type polynomial map over ℂ\mathbb{C} is globally invertible. We denote this conjecture in dimension nn as HC⁡(n)\mathrm{HC}(n), and restrict it to polynomial maps of exact degree d−1d-1 as HC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{HC}(n,d). In the early 2000s, Guowu Meng [7] established a fundamental bridge between the Hessian Conjecture and the classic Jacobian Conjecture, proving that HC⁡(2​n)\mathrm{HC}(2n) implies JC⁡(n)\mathrm{JC}(n) and, more specifically, that HC⁡(2​n,d+1)\mathrm{HC}(2n,d+1) implies JC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{JC}(n,d). The bridge was also obtained in [3], but here, we explicitly utilize Meng’s bridge (see also [4]). For instance, our counterexample to JC⁡(12,3)\mathrm{JC}(12,3), can be systematically converted into a concrete counterexample to HC⁡(24,4)\mathrm{HC}(24,4). This structural link was recently explored by Meng and Liang Yang [8], who applied these original reduction methods directly to Alpöge’s three-dimensional counterexample, thereby establishing the falsity of HC⁡(6)\mathrm{HC}(6) and HC⁡(6,8)\mathrm{HC}(6,8). Furthermore, in the same work, the authors successfully optimized their six-dimensional construction by exploiting the relatively simple underling structure of Alpöge’s map, ultimately improving the boundary to achieve a highly compact counterexample to HC⁡(5)\mathrm{HC}(5) and HC⁡(5,14)\mathrm{HC}(5,14).

When these stable mappings are passed to the differential gradient domain via the Hessian reduction rules established in Section 3, they generate definitive counterexamples to the Vanishing Conjecture. Under the standard dimension-doubling embedding, our direct homogeneous method transforms the counterexample against HJC⁡(15)\mathrm{HJC}(15) into a uniform potential establishing the falsity of HVC⁡(30)\mathrm{HVC}(30). In parallel, our optimized cubic–homogeneous BCW path lifts the counterexample against HJC⁡(18,3)\mathrm{HJC}(18,3) to drive a uniform potential establishing the falsity of HVC⁡(36,4)\mathrm{HVC}(36,4).

Finally, it is crucial to observe that global homogeneity is by no means mathematically required to invalidate the Vanishing Conjecture; according to Zhao’s general duality framework, a strict unipotent matrix structure is completely sufficient. By dropping the projectivized scale plane tt, our direct stabilization track yields a non-homogeneous map establishing the falsity of UJC⁡(14)\mathrm{UJC}(14), which under the complexified gradient reduction transforms into a potential establishing the falsity of VC⁡(28)\mathrm{VC}(28). In parallel, our optimized BCW path drives a non-homogeneous map establishing the falsity of UJC⁡(17,3)\mathrm{UJC}(17,3), which lifts to a potential establishing the falsity of VC⁡(34,4)\mathrm{VC}(34,4).

Crucially, all counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture and Hessian Conjecture presented throughout this work are defined strictly over the integers, ensuring arithmetic and numerical purity. Furthermore, all presented counterexamples to the Vanishing Conjecture are strictly over the Gaussian integers.

As an encore, we demonstrate in section 5 how our 18-dimensional cubic–homogeneous unipotent counterexample can be systematically funnelled into a strictly cubic–linear structure of Drużkowski type. For homogeneous counterexamples against HJC⁡(n,d)\mathrm{HJC}(n,d) where the terminal coordinate is isolated as xnx_{n}, a powerful classification theorem can be deployed to determine a feasible dimension for a corresponding stable power-linear mapping of degree dd. Applying this theorem with d=3d=3 directly to our structure allows us to chart a mathematically streamlined linearization pathway. However, while our previous term-by-term puzzles successfully mitigated variable inflation, the algebraic transition required to fully linearize the arguments of these cubic monomials still demands a massive expansion of the underlying coordinate framework. By executing this layered sequence of linear substitutions, the system is driven into a record-low, yet inherently expensive dimension of 90. This secondary reduction highlights that while intermediate unipotent rings can be tightly compressed, the final descent to pure Drużkowski linearity inevitably triggers a severe monomial expansion explosion.

Beyond the immediate structural breakthroughs, the exact numerical descent of our power-linear dimensions uncovered a series of remarkable historical and biographical parallels within the Jacobian framework. Prior to our awareness of Van Rijn’s result, our initial baseline Drużkowski linearization stood firmly at 123 variables. When the integration of our optimal 18-dimensional homogeneous map first compressed this boundary down to exactly 99 variables, it mirrored a famous numerical milestone from the doctoral work of Engelbert Hubbers. In his 1998 PhD thesis, Hubbers stabilized Pinchuk’s counterexample to the Strong Real Jacobian Conjecture to a cubic–linear mapping in dimension 2033, which he subsequently optimized in 1999 to exactly dimension 1999 (notice that any real-valued counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture is also a counterexample to the Strong Real Jacobian Conjecture). Although this structural coincidence dissolved about a week later when our polarization refinements drove the bound down to 98, a second historical resonance manifested when subsequent algebraic pruning collapsed the variable space to exactly 91 dimensions. This number matched an April Fools’ prank orchestrated by Arno van den Essen in 2006, who had sent an email to prominent researchers in the field claiming that the author had discovered a counterexample in dimension 91—owing to the fact that April 1st represents the 91st day of 2006 as a standard calendar year. Remarkably, even this final playful correspondence was bound to be overtaken by the algebraic reality of the counterexample: again about a week later, the boundary collapsed to its definitive minimum of 90, a historic threshold that mirrors the exact day of Van den Essen’s original email transmission on March 30th, the 90th day of 2006.

1.1 The Base Mapping and Volume-Preserving Transformation

To initialize our reduction framework, we examine Alpöge’s original three-dimensional counterexample F:ℂ3→ℂ3F:\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3}, defined as:

F1\displaystyle F_{1} =(1+x1​x2)3​x3+x22​(1+x1​x2)​(4+3​x1​x2)\displaystyle=(1+x_{1}x_{2})^{3}x_{3}+x_{2}^{2}(1+x_{1}x_{2})(4+3x_{1}x_{2}) (2)
F2\displaystyle F_{2} =x2+3​x1​(1+x1​x2)2​x3+3​x1​x22​(4+3​x1​x2)\displaystyle=x_{2}+3x_{1}(1+x_{1}x_{2})^{2}x_{3}+3x_{1}x_{2}^{2}(4+3x_{1}x_{2}) (3)
F3\displaystyle F_{3} =2​x1−3​x12​x2−x13​x3\displaystyle=2x_{1}-3x_{1}^{2}x_{2}-x_{1}^{3}x_{3} (4)

Expanding the determinant of its Jacobian yields det𝒥⁡(F)=−2\det\mathcal{J}(F)=-2. Thus, Alpöge’s mapping multiplies the volume by 22 and flips the orientation of the configuration space.

To bring this mapping into perfect harmony with standard unipotent reduction, we tweak Alpöge’s map to construct a volume- and orientation-preserving variant whose linear part is exactly the identity matrix. We define our initial transformed Keller map G:ℂ3→ℂ3G:\mathbb{C}^{3}\to\mathbb{C}^{3} analytically via the relation:

G⁡(x1,x2,x3)=12​(F3​(x1,2​x2,2​x3),F2​(x1,2​x2,2​x3),F1​(x1,2​x2,2​x3))G(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=\frac{1}{2}\Big(F_{3}(x_{1},2x_{2},2x_{3}),\,F_{2}(x_{1},2x_{2},2x_{3}),\,F_{1}(x_{1},2x_{2},2x_{3})\Big) (5)

Evaluating this composition explicitly yields the three-dimensional base map for our reduction sequence:

G1\displaystyle G_{1} =x1−3​x12​x2−x13​x3\displaystyle=x_{1}-3x_{1}^{2}x_{2}-x_{1}^{3}x_{3} (6)
G2\displaystyle G_{2} =3​v2​x1​x3+(9​v2−6​v−2)​x2\displaystyle=3v^{2}x_{1}x_{3}+(9v^{2}-6v-2)x_{2} (7)
G3\displaystyle G_{3} =v3​x3+(6​v2+2​v)​x22\displaystyle=v^{3}x_{3}+(6v^{2}+2v)x_{2}^{2} (8)

where v=1+2​x1​x2v=1+2x_{1}x_{2}. The structural validity and coordinate properties of this identity mapping have been fully verified.

1.2 Numerical Collision Universality and Parameterized Loci

Because the linear part of GG is the identity matrix, the geometric locus exhibits a non-injective failure where multiple preimages collapse into identical target zones. By evaluating the kernel split analytically, we isolate two distinct, parameterized collision paths running along the coordinate axes:

  1. 1.

    Collision Locus on the Third Axis: Along the third coordinate axis, the target collision path can be parameterized as (0, 0,t2)(0,\,0,\,\frac{t}{2}). For any non-zero parameter tt, this destination possesses three distinct preimages in the domain:

    {(0, 0,t2),(−t2​t,3​−t2,−13​t),(−−t2​t,−3​−t2,−13​t)}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\left\{\left(0,\,0,\,\frac{t}{2}\right),\;\left(\frac{\sqrt{-t}}{2t},\,\frac{3\sqrt{-t}}{2},\,-13t\right),\;\left(-\frac{\sqrt{-t}}{2t},\,-\frac{3\sqrt{-t}}{2},\,-13t\right)\right\} (9)

    Specializing this system by substituting t=−14t=-\frac{1}{4} yields the target point (0, 0,−18)(0,\,0,\,-\frac{1}{8}) with the three distinct preimages:

    {(0, 0,−18),(−1,34,134),(1,−34,134)}\left\{\left(0,\,0,\,-\frac{1}{8}\right),\;\left(-1,\,\frac{3}{4},\,\frac{13}{4}\right),\;\left(1,\,-\frac{3}{4},\,\frac{13}{4}\right)\right\} (10)

    which corresponds precisely to the transformation and normalization of Alpöge’s original non-injective collision coordinates.

  2. 2.

    Collision Locus on the Second Axis: Alternatively, the target path along the second coordinate axis is parameterized via (0,t2, 0)(0,\,\frac{t}{2},\,0). This family tracks a collapse where three distinct preimages map onto the single axis destination:

    {(0,t2,−2​t2),(−2t,t2,t2),(2t,−t4,5​t28)}\left\{\left(0,\,\frac{t}{2},\,-2t^{2}\right),\;\left(-\frac{2}{t},\,\frac{t}{2},\,t^{2}\right),\;\left(\frac{2}{t},\,-\frac{t}{4},\,\frac{5t^{2}}{8}\right)\right\} (11)

    Specializing this configuration by substituting t=2t=2 collapses the locus into the target destination (0, 1, 0)(0,\,1,\,0) and generates three distinct preimages, two of which are strictly integral:

    {(0, 1,−8),(−1, 1, 4),(1,−12,52)}\left\{\left(0,\,1,\,-8\right),\;\left(-1,\,1,\,4\right),\;\left(1,\,-\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{5}{2}\right)\right\} (12)

    which highlights the rich geometric layout of our base configuration.

The above coordinate collisions are formally verified within the accompanying Maxima worksheet section1.mac, along with the corresponding collisions of Alpöge’s original counterexample. The existence of these coordinate collisions establishes the absolute validity of the three-dimensional counterexample. In the following sections, we demonstrate how these non-injective loci are embedded and stabilized into higher-dimensional unipotent gradient rings, driving the explicit failure of the Vanishing Conjecture.

2 Reduction to a Unipotent Map

In this section, we establish the algebraic framework required to transform an arbitrary counterexample of the three-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture into a higher-dimensional polynomial map whose Jacobian matrix is unipotent. We provide a structural theorem addressing both the non-homogeneous and homogeneous cases, and formalize the stabilization procedure.

2.1 The Unipotent Reduction Theorem

Let RR be a commutative ring, and let X=(x1,x2,…,xn)X=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}) denote the standard coordinates in RnR^{n}. We consider polynomial maps F:Rn→RnF:R^{n}\to R^{n} of the form F=(F1,F2,…,Fn)F=(F_{1},F_{2},\dots,F_{n}), where each Fi∈R⁡[X]F_{i}\in R[X].

Definition 2.1 ((Homogeneous) Unipotent Polynomial Map).

A polynomial map F:Rn→RnF:R^{n}\to R^{n} is said to be a (homogeneous) unipotent polynomial map if it can be written in the form:

F⁡(X)=X+H⁡(X)F(X)=X+H(X) (13)

where H⁡(X)=(H1,H2,…,Hn)H(X)=(H_{1},H_{2},\dots,H_{n}) is a (homogeneous) polynomial vector field whose Jacobian matrix 𝒥⁡(H)\mathcal{J}(H) is strictly nilpotent. In the non-homogeneous setting, H⁡(X)H(X) may contain non-zero constant or linear terms. The identity matrix guarantees that 𝒥⁡(F)=In+𝒥⁡(H)\mathcal{J}(F)=I_{n}+\mathcal{J}(H) remains unipotent.

Traditional reduction techniques, such as the Bass-Connell-Wright (BCW) reduction, systematically force the degree of a Keller map down to 33. However, this process might introduce a severe inflation of dummy variables, expanding the dimension exponentially. By relaxing the target degree bound and accepting higher-degree structures, we can introduce a controlled stabilization that preserves a significantly lower dimension.

Theorem 2.2 (Unipotent Reduction and Exact Dimension Stabilization).

Let F:Rn→RnF:R^{n}\to R^{n} be a polynomial map whose linear part is the identity map, and let dd be a target degree such that d≥max⁡(deg⁡(F),2)d\geq\max(\deg(F),2).

  1. 1.

    Non-Homogeneous Case: There exists an explicit algebraic stabilization that constructs a polynomial map G:Rm→RmG:R^{m}\to R^{m} of degree dd, where the exact stable dimension mm is given by:

    m=n+∑i=1nmax⁡(deg⁡(Fi)−2,0)m=n+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\max(\deg(F_{i})-2,0) (14)

    such that for H=G−XH=G-X:

    det(𝒥⁡((X+t​H))=(det(𝒥​F))|X=t​XCLOSE\det\big(\mathcal{J}((X+tH)\big)=\big(\det(\mathcal{J}F)\big)\big|_{X=tX} (15)

    where X=(x1,x2,…,xm)X=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m}).

    Furthermore, for each p∈Rnp\in R^{n}, there exists q∈R​[t]mq\in R[t]^{m} of the form (t​p,∗,…,∗)(tp,*,\ldots,*), with coordinates n+1,n+2,…,mn+1,n+2,\ldots,m in R​t2∪⋯∪R​td−1R\,t^{2}\cup\cdots\cup R\,t^{d-1}, such that

    (X+t−1​H)​(q)=(t​F​(p),0,…,0)\big(X+t^{-1}H)(q)=(t\,F(p),0,\ldots,0) (16)

    In particular, q|t=1=(p,∗,…,∗)q|_{t=1}=(p,*,\ldots,*) and G⁡(q|t=1)=(F⁡(p),0,…,0)G(q|_{t=1})=(F(p),0,\ldots,0).

  2. 2.

    Homogeneous Case: There exists an explicit extension of this stabilization that constructs a strictly homogeneous unipotent map Gh:Rm+1→Rm+1G_{h}:R^{m+1}\to R^{m+1} of degree dd by introducing exactly one additional global homogenizing variable, elevating the exact dimension to m+1m+1, such that for Hh=Gh−XhH_{h}=G_{h}-X_{h}:

    det(𝒥⁡(Xh+t​Hh))=(det(𝒥​F))|Xh=t​xm+1d−2​Xh\det\big(\mathcal{J}(X_{h}+tH_{h})\big)=\big(\det(\mathcal{J}F)\big)\big|_{X_{h}=tx_{m+1}^{d-2}X_{h}} (17)

    and (Hh)m+1=0(H_{h})_{m+1}=0, where Xh=(x1,x2,…,xm,xm+1)X_{h}=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{m},x_{m+1}).

    Furthermore, for each p∈Rnp\in R^{n}, there exists qh∈R​[t]m+1q_{h}\in R[t]^{m+1} of the form (t​p,∗,…,∗,1)(tp,*,\ldots,*,1), with coordinates n+1,n+2,…,mn+1,n+2,\ldots,m in R​t2∪⋯∪R​td−1R\,t^{2}\cup\cdots\cup R\,t^{d-1}, such that

    (Xh+t−1​Hh)​(qh)=(t​F​(p),0,…,0,1)(X_{h}+t^{-1}H_{h})(q_{h})=(t\,F(p),0,\ldots,0,1) (18)

    In particular, qh|t=1=(p,∗,…,∗,1)q_{h}|_{t=1}=(p,*,\ldots,*,1) and Gh​(qh|t=1)=(F⁡(p),0,…,0,1)G_{h}(q_{h}|_{t=1})=(F(p),0,\ldots,0,1).

Corollary 2.3.

If the polynomial map FF in Theorem 2.2 possesses a constant Jacobian determinant, then det𝒥⁡(F)=1\det\mathcal{J}(F)=1 and the stabilized mappings GG and GhG_{h} are strictly unipotent Jacobian maps. That is, the Jacobian matrices 𝒥⁡(H)\mathcal{J}(H) and 𝒥⁡(Hh)\mathcal{J}(H_{h}) are strictly nilpotent.

Proof.

As the linear part of FF is XX, det𝒥⁡(F)=1\det\mathcal{J}(F)=1 follows. We first address the non-homogeneous mapping G:Rm→RmG:R^{m}\to R^{m} with H=G−XH=G-X. By substituting the condition det𝒥⁡(F)=1\det\mathcal{J}(F)=1 into the matrix relation of Theorem 2.2, the characteristic polynomial of 𝒥⁡(H)\mathcal{J}(H) collapses via the identity:

tm\displaystyle t^{m} =tm⋅1|t=−t−1=tm⋅(det𝒥⁡(X+t​H))|t=−t−1\displaystyle=t^{m}\cdot 1\big|_{t=-t^{-1}}=t^{m}\cdot\big(\det\mathcal{J}(X+tH)\big)\big|_{t=-t^{-1}}

2.2 Construction of the stabilization

To manipulate the degrees of these mappings dynamically without disrupting invertibility conditions, we embed the system into a polynomial ring extended by a homogenization parameter tt. This parameter controls the scaling of the highest-degree homogeneous components during the iterative dimension-raising steps.

Because each successive reduction step introduces a new coordinate linked to a specific higher-degree term, the process proceeds without gaps, allowing for an exact determination of the stable dimension.

We construct the map GG of dimension mm iteratively by resolving components whose degrees exceed the targeted bound dd. To establish a uniform grading profile, we embed the system into the extended ring R​[t]​[X]R[t][X] by evaluating the initial map under a tt-deformed scale:

Under this transformation, a homogeneous component of FF of degree jj acquires a total degree of j⁡(d−2)−(d−2)=(j−1)​(d−2)+1j(d-2)-(d-2)=(j-1)(d-2)+1 in GG for j=1,2,…,dj=1,2,\ldots,d. This shows that while gaps exist between these allowed degree profiles, the structure of the grading is strictly preserved under the scaling operation.

Suppose a component GiG_{i} has a maximum total degree k=deg⁡(Gi)>dk=\deg(G_{i})>d. We extract its leading homogeneous part of degree kk, denoted here as Gi(k)G_{i}^{(k)}. We introduce a new auxiliary variable xm+1x_{m+1} and append the new coordinate relation hh defined as:

h=xm+1+Gi(k)tk−dh=x_{m+1}+\frac{G_{i}^{(k)}}{t^{k-d}} (22)

Notice that because Gi(k)G_{i}^{(k)} is homogeneous of degree kk, the fraction possesses a total degree of k−(k−d)=dk-(k-d)=d. The component hh therefore consists exclusively of terms of degree 11 (from xm+1x_{m+1}) and degree dd (from the fraction), maintaining a single gap of size d−1d-1 within the appended relation.

By appending hh to GG as a new coordinate condition, we can subtract the leading high-degree contribution from the original component via the replacement:

Gi←Gi−h⋅tk−d=Gi−Gi(k)−xm+1​tk−dG_{i}\leftarrow G_{i}-h\cdot t^{k-d}=G_{i}-G_{i}^{(k)}-x_{m+1}t^{k-d} (23)

This substitution completely annihilates the leading homogeneous part Gi(k)G_{i}^{(k)} of degree kk. The remaining newly introduced term, −xm+1​tk−d-x_{m+1}t^{k-d}, has a total degree of exact size 1+(k−d)=k−d+11+(k-d)=k-d+1.

The maximum degree of this component has therefore decreased from kk to k−d+1k-d+1, which represents a strict reduction of exactly k−(k−d+1)=d−1k-(k-d+1)=d-1. Furthermore, because xm+1x_{m+1} is a fresh variable, it cannot interact with or be canceled by any pre-existing terms in GiG_{i}, guaranteeing that the degree drops by exactly d−1d-1.

Since each step reduces the target degree by this uniform invariant without generating irregular intermediate degree patterns, the iteration terminates precisely when all components satisfy the degree bound dd. This gap-free reduction sequence yields the exact stable final dimension of m=n+∑max⁡(deg⁡(Fi)−2,0)m=n+\sum\max(\deg(F_{i})-2,0).

For the non-homogeneous mapping, setting t=1t=1 specializes the system back to RmR^{m}. For the homogeneous mapping, substituting the parameter tt with the (m+1)(m+1)-th coordinate xm+1x_{m+1} synchronizes the degrees, generating a perfectly uniform homogeneous profile of degree dd across all m+1m+1 components.

Note that in the non-homogeneous setting, the resulting unipotent map may contain linear terms other than those of its identity linear part, as a consequence of stabilizing higher-degree cross-terms.

3 Reduction to Hessian-Type Maps and Zhao’s Vanishing Conjecture

In this section, we transition from stable unipotent polynomial automorphisms to gradient maps of Hessian type. We first define a parameterized symmetric potential over the polynomial ring ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t] and evaluate its exact determinental profile. We then invoke Wenhua Zhao’s duality theorem to establish that the core potential hh constitutes a definitive counterexample to the Vanishing Conjecture (VC).

3.1 The Parameterized Symmetric Potential and Determinant Valuation

Let SS be a commutative ring with an element ii such that i2+1=0i^{2}+1=0. Let F:Sn→SnF:S^{n}\to S^{n} be a stabilized unipotent polynomial map written as F⁡(X)=X+H⁡(X)F(X)=X+H(X), where 𝒥⁡(H)\mathcal{J}(H) is a nilpotent matrix. To analyze the behavioral deformation under linear scaling, we lift the system to a polynomial ring extended by a formal variable tt, considering the parameterized mapping over S​[t]​[X]S[t][X] defined as:

Ft​(X)=t​X+H⁡(X)F_{t}(X)=tX+H(X) (32)

Following the symmetric gradient reduction framework established by de Bondt and van den Essen [3], we duplicate the dimension of the coordinate space by spanning a 2​n2n-dimensional affine structure with coordinates (X,Y)=(x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn)∈S2​n(X,Y)=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})\in S^{2n}. We invoke the complexified independent linear frames zj=xj+i​yjz_{j}=x_{j}+iy_{j} and their geoconjugate counters z¯j=xj−i​yj\bar{z}_{j}=x_{j}-iy_{j}. We define the structural symmetric potential gt​(X,Y)∈S⁡[t]​[X,Y]g_{t}(X,Y)\in S[t][X,Y] via the inner product pairing:

gt​(X,Y):=∑j=1nz¯j⋅(Ft)j​(z)=t​∑j=1nz¯j​zj+∑j=1nz¯j​Hj​(z)g_{t}(X,Y):=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bar{z}_{j}\cdot(F_{t})_{j}(z)=t\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bar{z}_{j}z_{j}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bar{z}_{j}H_{j}(z) (33)

which is of the form:

where h⁡(X,Y)=∑j=1nz¯j​Hj​(Z)h(X,Y)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bar{z}_{j}H_{j}(Z). Taking the real gradient of this full potential yields the parameterized Hessian mapping 𝒢t=∇gt:S2​n→S2​n\mathcal{G}_{t}=\nabla g_{t}:S^{2n}\to S^{2n}:

Theorem 3.1 (Determinant Invariance of the Symmetric Map).

Let gt​(X,Y)=t​∑(xj2+yj2)+h⁡(X,Y)g_{t}(X,\allowbreak Y)=t\sum(x_{j}^{2}+y_{j}^{2})+h(X,Y) be the parameterized potential generated by the deformed map Ft=t​X+H⁡(X)F_{t}=tX+H(X). Consequently, if 12∈S\frac{1}{2}\in S, then for any specialized value t∈S×t\in S^{\times}, the Jacobian determinant of the mapping 𝒢t​(X,Y)=2​t​(X,Y)+∇h​(X,Y)\mathcal{G}_{t}(X,Y)=2t(X,Y)+\nabla h(X,Y) is an invertible constant (which is the deteminant condition of the Jacobian conjecture).

Because the bottom-right block is identically zero, the determinant collapses to the product of its off-diagonal blocks:

detℋZ,Z¯​(gt)=(−1)n​(tn)2=(−1)n​t2​n\det\mathcal{H}_{Z,\bar{Z}}(g_{t})=(-1)^{n}(t^{n})^{2}=(-1)^{n}t^{2n} (42)

This confirms that for any specialization t∈ℂ×t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}, the determinant is a non-vanishing constant, preserving the global Keller condition globally. ∎

3.2 Connection between the Vanishing Conjecture and the Unipotent Jacobian Conjecture

We begin by establishing the formal duality framework introduced by Wenhua Zhao [10], which connects the differential criteria of the Laplace operator to the unipotent inversion framework. Zhao established that if a polynomial potential P∈ℂ⁡[X]P\in\mathbb{C}[X] contains no terms of total degree ≤1\leq 1, then PP serves as a counterexample to the Vanishing Conjecture if and only if the parameterized polynomial mapping Ft(X)=X−t∇PF_{t}(X)=X-t\nabla P constitutes a counterexample to the unipotent Jacobian Conjecture over the polynomial ring ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t].

For our structural analysis, we observe that operating with the map X−t∇PX-t\nabla P is algebraically equivalent to operating with X+t∇PX+t\nabla P under a sign-inversion of the parameter space. To rigorously specialize this parameterized family into standalone numerical counterexamples over the base ring without risk of coordinate coalescence, one can deploy the following general theorem, which applies to polynomial mappings whose Jacobian matrices are not required to be symmetric.

Theorem 3.2.

Let RR be a commutative ring, let X=(x1,…,xn)X=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) denote the coordinate vector, and let H:Rn→RnH:R^{n}\to R^{n} be a polynomial vector field. We consider the parameterized polynomial mapping X+t​HX+tH defined over the polynomial ring R⁡[t]R[t].

  1. 1.

    If there exists a scalar element λ∈R\lambda\in R such that the specialized numerical mapping X+λ​HX+\lambda H is not globally invertible over RR, then the parameterized mapping X+t​HX+tH is not globally invertible over R⁡[t]R[t].

  2. 2.

    If 𝒥⁡(H)\mathcal{J}(H) is strictly nilpotent, then the linear part of X+t​HX+tH is globally invertible over R⁡[t]R[t].

  3. 3.

    If RR is a reduced ring where the zero polynomial is the unique polynomial over RR that evaluates identically to the zero function, and X+t​HX+tH is not globally invertible over R⁡[t]R[t] while the linear part of X+t​HX+tH is globally invertible over R⁡[t]R[t], then there exist infinitely many scalar values λ∈R\lambda\in R such that the specialized mapping X+λ​HX+\lambda H is not globally invertible over RR.

  4. 4.

    If X+t​HX+tH is not globally invertible over R⁡[t]R[t] and the vector field HH is strictly homogeneous of degree d≥2d\geq 2, then for every element λ∈R\lambda\in R that is not a zero-divisor, the specialized mapping X+λ​HX+\lambda H is not globally invertible over RR.

Proof.
  1. 1.

    We prove the assertion by contraposition. Suppose the parameterized mapping X+t​HX+tH is globally invertible over R⁡[t]R[t] with a well-defined polynomial inverse G⁡(X,t)G(X,t). Specializing the parameter value by substituting t=λt=\lambda yields the polynomial map G⁡(X,λ)G(X,\lambda), which acts as the exact global inverse of the specialized map X+λ​HX+\lambda H over RR, contradicting the non-invertibility assumption.

  2. 2.

    To establish the global invertibility of the linear part of X+t​HX+tH over R⁡[t]R[t], we examine its constant Jacobian configuration evaluated at the origin X=0X=0. The linear multiplier matrix of the parameterized system is given explicitly by A=In+t​𝒥​(H)|X=0A=I_{n}+t\mathcal{J}(H)|_{X=0}. Because the Jacobian matrix 𝒥⁡(H)\mathcal{J}(H) is strictly nilpotent by assumption, its evaluation 𝒥⁡(H)|X=0\mathcal{J}(H)|_{X=0} is likewise a nilpotent matrix over RR, meaning there exists a minimal packing index k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that (𝒥⁡(H)|X=0)k=0(\mathcal{J}(H)|_{X=0})^{k}=0.

    Consequently, we can construct the formal inverse matrix via a finite Neumann series expansion:

    A−1\displaystyle A^{-1} =In−t⁡(𝒥⁡(H)|X=0)+t2​(𝒥⁡(H)|X=0)2−\displaystyle=I_{n}-t\big(\mathcal{J}(H)\big|_{X=0}\big)+t^{2}\big(\mathcal{J}(H)\big|_{X=0}\big)^{2}-{}
    t3​(𝒥⁡(H)|X=0)3+⋯±tk−1​(𝒥⁡(H)|X=0)k−1\displaystyle\qquad t^{3}\big(\mathcal{J}(H)\big|_{X=0}\big)^{3}+\dots\pm t^{k-1}\big(\mathcal{J}(H)\big|_{X=0}\big)^{k-1} (44)

    Since this matrix summation terminates at a finite degree tk−1t^{k-1}, all its entries are strictly polynomial components contained within the ring R⁡[t]R[t]. Evaluating the product verifies that A⋅A−1=InA\cdot A^{-1}=I_{n}. Because the linear part possesses a well-defined, polynomial inverse matrix over R⁡[t]R[t], it is globally invertible over the domain R⁡[t]R[t], completing the proof.

  3. 3.

    Just as above, A=In+t​𝒥​(H)|X=0A=I_{n}+t\mathcal{J}(H)|_{X=0} denotes the matrix representing the linear part of the parameterized mapping X+t​HX+tH. Since AA is invertible, the exact inverse of AA over RR exists, and we denote it by A−1A^{-1}. We define the modified polynomial mapping

    Φ⁡(X,t)=A⋅(X+t⁡(H−H⁡(0)))\Phi(X,t)=A\cdot\big(X+t(H-H(0))\big)

    By construction, the Jacobian matrix of this composition satisfies 𝒥⁡(Φ)|X=0=A−1​A=In\mathcal{J}(\Phi)|_{X=0}=A^{-1}A=I_{n}, meaning the constant part of the Jacobian determinant is normalized to the identity matrix. Since X+t​HX+tH is not globally invertible, the composition Φ⁡(X,t)\Phi(X,t) is likewise non-invertible.

    According to the formal inversion criterion for polynomial automorphisms, the formal power series inverse of Φ⁡(X,t)\Phi(X,t) must contain at least one non-vanishing higher-order term whose total degree strictly exceeds the standard geometric bound dn−1d^{n-1}, where d=maxi⁡(deg⁡Φi)d=\max_{i}(\deg\Phi_{i}). The coefficient of this higher-order term can be isolated as a non-zero polynomial f⁡(t)∈R⁡[t]f(t)\in R[t]. Since RR respects the functional identity property where the zero polynomial is the unique representative of the zero function, there must exist a scalar value λ∈R\lambda\in R such that f⁡(λ)≠0f(\lambda)\neq 0. This implies that the formal power series inverse of the specialized mapping Φ⁡(X,λ)\Phi(X,\lambda) retains a non-vanishing term beyond the geometric degree bound, proving that X+λ​HX+\lambda H is not globally invertible over RR. Furthermore, since the modified polynomial (t−λ)​f​(t)∈R⁡[t](t-\lambda)f(t)\in R[t] is non-zero, there must exist a distinct scalar value λ′≠λ\lambda^{\prime}\neq\lambda such that f⁡(λ′)≠0f(\lambda^{\prime})\neq 0, generating a distinct non-invertible specialized map. Repeating this construction inductively establishes the existence of infinitely many non-invertible scalar specializations over RR.

  4. 4.

    We prove the assertion by contraposition. Suppose there exists an element λ∈R\lambda\in R that is not a zero-divisor such that the specialized numerical mapping X+λ​HX+\lambda H is globally invertible over RR. Because the vector field HH is strictly homogeneous of degree d≥2d\geq 2, applying the coordinate rescaling X←t​XX\leftarrow tX yields the homogeneity relation H⁡(t​X)=td​H​(X)H(tX)=t^{d}H(X). It follows that the projectivized map t−1​(t​X+λ​H​(t​X))=X+td−1​λ​H​(X)t^{-1}(tX+\lambda H(tX))=X+t^{d-1}\lambda H(X) is globally invertible over the polynomial ring R⁡[td−1​λ]R[t^{d-1}\lambda]. Consequently, X+t​λ​H​(X)X+t\lambda H(X) is globally invertible over the polynomial ring R⁡[t​λ]R[t\lambda].

    To lift this property to the full polynomial ring R⁡[t]R[t], we construct the multiplicative set Λ={λ,λ2,λ3,…}\Lambda=\{\lambda,\lambda^{2},\lambda^{3},\dots\}. Since λ\lambda is not a zero-divisor, Λ\Lambda contains no zero-divisors, making the canonical localization homomorphism from RR into the ring of fractions Λ−1​R\Lambda^{-1}R strictly injective. We may therefore naturally view R⁡[t]R[t] as a subring of the localized polynomial ring (Λ−1​R)​[t](\Lambda^{-1}R)[t]. Over this localized domain, the element λ\lambda is a unit. We can then define the localized ring endomorphism ϕ:(Λ−1​R)​[t]→(Λ−1​R)​[t]\phi:(\Lambda^{-1}R)[t]\to(\Lambda^{-1}R)[t] determined by the mapping f⁡(t)↦f⁡(λ​t)f(t)\mapsto f(\lambda t). Because λ\lambda is invertible in Λ−1​R\Lambda^{-1}R, this endomorphism is a strict automorphism possessing the exact algebraic inverse ϕ−1:f⁡(t)↦f⁡(λ−1​t)\phi^{-1}:f(t)\mapsto f(\lambda^{-1}t). The restriction of ϕ\phi to R⁡[t]R[t] is therefore a strict isomorphism between R⁡[t]R[t] and R⁡[t​λ]R[t\lambda]. This forces the core parameterized mapping X+t​HX+tH to be globally invertible over the standard polynomial ring R⁡[t]R[t], completing the proof. ∎

Finally, this parameterized structure reveals a fundamental arithmetic trade-off inherent to the reduction ring. We can repair the underlying scalar potential by replacing the base ring ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i] by ℤ​[i]​[12]\mathbb{Z}[i][\frac{1}{2}].

4 Optimized Bass–Connell–Wright Reduction to Degree 3

In this section, we formalize an optimized version of the Bass–Connell–Wright (BCW) degree-reduction algorithm [2]. We present our reduction framework as an evolving multi-stage refinement. First, we outline our original reduction to degree 3 without homogeniety, which is a more straightforward baseline reduction sequence that establishes a clear, accessible path to degree 3, terminating at a stable cubic map of 14 variables. This reduction is executed in section4a.mac. While not achieving a record-low variable count, this 14-dimensional cubic framework is mathematically transparent and serves as the conceptual foundation.

In the subsequent subsections, we demonstrate how deeper insights into structural cofactors allow us to compress this space to 12 dimensions, by providing two additional reductions. The first reduction is essentially the same as that of Van Rijn. But the second reduction differs in that the subsequent reduction to cubic-homogeneous form, as outlined in section 2, ends in dimension 18 instead of 19.

4.1 Base Extension and Initial Monomial Grid

Let (G1,G2,G3)(G_{1},G_{2},G_{3}) be the volume-normalized three-dimensional counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture defined in Section 1. To initiate the reduction sequence, we expand the affine coordinate space by appending exactly seven baseline auxiliary components representing six monomials in x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}, and the monomial x2​x6x_{2}x_{6}. The core monomials are:

x12,x1​x2,x1​x3,x2​x6,x12​x3,x1​x22,x12​x2​x3x_{1}^{2},\,x_{1}x_{2},\,x_{1}x_{3},\,x_{2}x_{6},\;\;x_{1}^{2}x_{3},\,x_{1}x_{2}^{2},\;\;x_{1}^{2}x_{2}x_{3} (53)

By ordering these components strictly from highest to lowest total degree, we define the initial extended mapping vector:

G4\displaystyle G_{4} =x4+x12​x2​x3\displaystyle=x_{4}+x_{1}^{2}x_{2}x_{3} (54)
G5\displaystyle G_{5} =x5+x12​x3\displaystyle=x_{5}+x_{1}^{2}x_{3} (55)
G6\displaystyle G_{6} =x6+x1​x22\displaystyle=x_{6}+x_{1}x_{2}^{2} (56)
G7\displaystyle G_{7} =x7+x12\displaystyle=x_{7}+x_{1}^{2} (57)
G8\displaystyle G_{8} =x8+x1​x2\displaystyle=x_{8}+x_{1}x_{2} (58)
G9\displaystyle G_{9} =x9+x1​x3\displaystyle=x_{9}+x_{1}x_{3} (59)
G10\displaystyle G_{10} =x10+x2​x6\displaystyle=x_{10}+x_{2}x_{6} (60)

This forms our initial 10-dimensional extended polynomial mapping vector G=(G1,…,G10)G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{10}). The inclusion of the cross-interaction link G10=x10+x2​x6G_{10}=x_{10}+x_{2}x_{6} ensures that the network remains algebraically closed under localized factorizations.

4.2 The Monomial Factorization Loop and Early Termination

The reduction algorithm operates component-by-component over the first four dimensions of GG. For each component GcG_{c} (1≤c≤41\leq c\leq 4), the leading non-linear monomial MM (with total degree dd and scalar coefficient cMc_{M}) is captured sequentially. To minimize variable expansion, the core factorization loop differentiates between the components:

  • •

    For G1G_{1} and G4G_{4}, the loop runs iteratively until the component is reduced to degree 3.

  • •

    For G2G_{2} and G3G_{3}, the loop terminates early, leaving the components at degree 4.

During this loop, the selected monomial MM is evaluated to find a divisor within the initial grid of degree ⌈d/2⌉\lceil d/2\rceil. Because the grid is pre-optimized, the routine always locates a complete pair of indices [i,j][i,j] from the baseline set (1≤i,j≤71\leq i,j\leq 7) such that the product of the corresponding core monomials matches MM exactly. The component is then immediately updated via a direct factorization substitution:

Gc←Gc−cM⋅Gi+3⋅Gj+3G_{c}\leftarrow G_{c}-c_{M}\cdot G_{i+3}\cdot G_{j+3} (61)

where Gi+3G_{i+3} and Gj+3G_{j+3} represent the corresponding shifted variables from the baseline grid. Because the maximum degree of G4G_{4} is 44, its target ceiling bound is ⌈4/2⌉=2\lceil 4/2\rceil=2. Consequently, G4G_{4} will only look for quadratic grid links and can never select its own core monomial as a divisor, rendering circular definitions impossible.

4.3 The Secondary Quotient Sweeping Step for G2G_{2} and G3G_{3}

Because the primary factorization loop for G2G_{2} and G3G_{3} terminates at degree 4, these components require a dedicated secondary stabilization step to safely clear their remaining degree-4 excesses down to degree 3. This is achieved via exact algebraic polynomial division using the specific quadratic baseline anchors x1​x2x_{1}x_{2} and x1​x3x_{1}x_{3}:

  1. 1.

    The x𝟏​x𝟐x_{1}x_{2}-Quotient Sweep: The algorithm isolates the homogeneous degree-4 part of the active component and divides it by x1​x2x_{1}x_{2}. The resulting quotient (which is strictly of degree 2) is bound to a new auxiliary variable by incrementing the stable dimension m←m+1m\leftarrow m+1:

    Gm=xm+Q1G_{m}=x_{m}+Q_{1} (62)

    where Q1Q_{1} is the algebraic quotient. The component is then updated by subtracting the product of this new variable and the G8=x8+x1​x2G_{8}=x_{8}+x_{1}x_{2} grid anchor:

    Gc←Gc−G8⋅GmG_{c}\leftarrow G_{c}-G_{8}\cdot G_{m} (63)
  2. 2.

    Gm=xm+Q2G_{m}=x_{m}+Q_{2} (64)

Since both quotients are strictly quadratic, their multiplication with the quadratic baseline anchors generates pure degree-4 contributions that perfectly eliminate the highest-degree terms without introducing higher-order cross-contaminations, successfully forcing G2G_{2} and G3G_{3} to degree 3.

4.6 A Twelve-Dimensional Configuration with Five Cubic Components

Under the structural swap of F1F_{1} and the quartic monomial in the previous constructions, two cubic monomials remain sufficient to drive the reduction, though the configuration demands one additional quadratic monomial. Because this new quadratic block cannot be linearly combined with any existing core monomials, the system maintains a stable total count of exactly 12 components.

Furthermore, during the final transition forcing components F2F_{2} and F3F_{3} from degree 4 down to degree 3, only three remaining fourth-degree terms manifest across the network. By exploiting this low algebraic overhead, we successfully integrate the final sweeping steps directly into the core factorization reduction over the baseline grid, removing the necessity for an independent quotient elimination phase. Remark 4.1.

It is instructive to analyze the algebraic behavior of the first component F1F_{1} under the geometric locus. One might initially expect that the condition F1=0F_{1}=0, which holds at the parameterized coordinate destination, is the primary mechanism that prevents the non-injective collision points from being altered during the transformation. However, a precise tracking of the reduction sequence reveals that F1F_{1} is systematically multiplied by the auxiliary components F5F_{5} and F6F_{6} prior to the elimination phase. Because both F5F_{5} and F6F_{6} already vanish identically under the kernel initialization, their vanishing is completely sufficient to ensure that the coordinate vectors of the preimages are extended trivially by appending zeroes. Consequently, the condition F1=0F_{1}=0 is not important for the current elimination track.

Even if the duality vector EE had contained a pure y1y_{1}-term, such as y12y_{1}^{2}, the core injectivity failure would remain entirely unbroken, though it would shift the numerical coordinate positions of the specialized preimages within the extended domain.

4.7 The Resulting Stable Unipotent and Homogeneous Counterexamples

Following the reduction algorithms detailed above, the primary loop terminates successfully at our three structural milestones of 14, 12 (with six cubic components), and 12 (with five cubic components) variables, respectively. To lift these intermediate cubic mappings to their final stable configurations, we invoke the stabilization algorithms from Section 2. Because forcing uniform degrees across the networks depends linearly on the remaining degree-deficits, the stabilization branches into two completely equivalent pathways across all three frameworks:

  1. 1.

    The Non-Homogeneous Maps GG: Specializing the parameter configurations without enforcing global homogenization collapses the parameter spaces to exact final dimensions evaluated by the sum M=2​c+qM=2c+q, where cc represents the stabilized cubic variables and qq represents the quadratic-lifting parameters.

    • •

      For our initial 14-dimensional baseline map (c=6,q=8c=6,q=8), the dimension collapses to M=2×6+8=20M=2\times 6+8=20, yielding an explicit unipotent polynomial map G:ℂ20→ℂ20G:\mathbb{C}^{20}\to\mathbb{C}^{20} of degree 3 and a definitive 40-dimensional non-homogeneous counterexample of degree 4 to the Vanishing Conjecture.

    • •

      For our refined 12-dimensional map (c=6,q=6c=6,q=6), the dimension evaluates to M=2×6+6=18M=2\times 6+6=18, yielding an explicit unipotent polynomial map G:ℂ18→ℂ18G:\mathbb{C}^{18}\to\mathbb{C}^{18} of degree 3 and a definitive 36-dimensional non-homogeneous counterexample of degree 4 to the Vanishing Conjecture.

    • •

      For our optimal 12-dimensional map (c=5,q=7c=5,q=7), the dimension collapses to a record minimum of M=2×5+7=17M=2\times 5+7=17, yielding an explicit unipotent polynomial map G:ℂ17→ℂ17G:\mathbb{C}^{17}\to\mathbb{C}^{17} of degree 3 and a definitive 34-dimensional non-homogeneous counterexample of degree 4 to the Vanishing Conjecture.

  2. 2.

    The Homogeneous Maps GhG_{h}: Alternatively, enforcing strict uniformity of degree 3 under a global scale parameter adds exactly 1 synchronization axis to the core sum, elevating the total architectures to their final homogeneous dimensions:

    • •

      For our initial baseline framework, the dimension evaluates to M=2×6+8+1=21M=2\times 6+8+1=21, yielding an explicit homogeneous polynomial map Gh:ℂ21→ℂ21G_{h}:\mathbb{C}^{21}\to\mathbb{C}^{21} and a definitive 42-dimensional homogeneous counterexample of degree 4 to the Vanishing Conjecture.

    • •

      For our refined framework, the dimension collapses to M=2×6+6+1=19M=2\times 6+6+1=19, yielding an explicit homogeneous polynomial map Gh:ℂ19→ℂ19G_{h}:\mathbb{C}^{19}\to\mathbb{C}^{19} and a definitive 38-dimensional homogeneous counterexample of degree 4 to the Vanishing Conjecture.

    • •

      For our optimal framework, the dimension reaches an absolute structural limit of M=2×5+7+1=18M=2\times 5+7+1=18, yielding an explicit homogeneous polynomial map Gh:ℂ18→ℂ18G_{h}:\mathbb{C}^{18}\to\mathbb{C}^{18} and a definitive 36-dimensional homogeneous counterexample of degree 4 to the Vanishing Conjecture.

Due to the intensive variable tracking and multi-layered quotient alignments, the full polynomial expansions of these mappings are algebraically too large to be practically displayed here. The complete, uncurated coordinate configurations and automated verification scripts for our reductions are provided in the respective ancillary files section4a.mac, section4b.mac and section4c.mac.

5 The Descent to Drużkowski Cubic–Linearity

In this section, we transition from stable unipotent coordinate frameworks to strictly power-linear structures of Drużkowski type. To systematically chart the algebraic path toward linearization and prepare the system for subsequent minimization, we introduce a general reduction mechanism that establishes a clear dimensional upper bound for the resulting linear variable space. Crucially, this reduction framework operates universally for any arbitrary system degree d≥2d\geq 2, allowing higher-degree homogeneous mappings to be driven down to pure linearity without requiring restrictive low-degree assumptions at the core.

5.1 The Power-Linear Reduction Theorem

To save one stabilization dimension without tweaking the cubic–homogeneous map GG in advance, we do not work directly with the vector field G⁡(X)G(X) itself. Instead, we embed our counterexample into a modified cubic–linear framework by applying a pairing technique specifically to the perturbed mapping G⁡(X)+xnd​enG(X)+x_{n}^{d}e_{n}, which isolates the final coordinate axis as an explicit higher-order generator. Although our reduction builds upon structural concepts originally introduced by Gorni and Zampieri [5], the reduction procedure and the proof of Theorem 5.1 are entirely self-contained, depending strictly on the inner algebraic properties of our specific coordinate representations.

Let B∈Rn×mB\in R^{n\times m} be the coefficient matrix defined by H=B​𝑃𝐿H=B\,\mathit{PL}. If BB is right-invertible, and the last row of BB contains an entry in R×R^{\times}, then there exists a Drużkowski-type stabilization of GG in exactly dimension mm.

Remark 5.2.

To see explicitly how this construction saves a stabilization dimension, consider the algebraic interplay between the final component and the rank condition. Because the original map satisfies Gn​(X)=xnG_{n}(X)=x_{n}, its intrinsic cubic part is identically zero, meaning that without modification, the nn-th component of the target map would satisfy Hn=0H_{n}=0. If the matrix BB is to maintain full rank nn, the fact that Hn=0H_{n}=0 mathematically forces the existence of a non-trivial linear relation among the components of the cubic-linear power map 𝑃𝐿\mathit{PL} to prevent a row of zeroes.

Furthermore, this explanation clarifies why we do not need to pre-emptively alter the system. If xndx_{n}^{d} were already a component of 𝑃𝐿\mathit{PL}, one could tweak the cubic-homogeneous map GG in advance to avoid generating xndx_{n}^{d} entirely. This would naturally save a dimension as well, without the need to apply the Gorni-Zampieri pairing on G⁡(X)+xnd​enG(X)+x_{n}^{d}e_{n} instead of G⁡(X)G(X).

Remark 5.3.

Although Theorem 5.1 establishes the existence of a Drużkowski counterexample in dimension mm, it does not automatically guarantee that mm is the absolute minimal dimension achievable. However, if the resulting Drużkowski map is constructed directly from GG and the polynomial map 𝑃𝐿\mathit{PL}, one can reasonably expect that all individual components of 𝑃𝐿\mathit{PL} manifest themselves in a transparent, structural manner within the final cubic-linear framework.

Under the assumption that no linear dependencies exist between the components of 𝑃𝐿\mathit{PL}, the condition that BB is right-invertible implies that the components of HH are linearly independent. While this allows for the explicit generation of xndx_{n}^{d}, any further reduction in dimension would necessitate a non-trivial linear intertwining of the independent powers. Consequently, assuming that the essential linear transformations of the components of 𝑃𝐿\mathit{PL} must be preserved within the cubic parts of the Drużkowski map, all mm dimensions are strictly required, making the dimension tight for this specific stabilization framework.

Remark 5.4.

It is highly instructive to evaluate these power-linear reductions from a ring-theoretic perspective by generalizing the Drużkowski transformation to commutative Hermite rings. While our unipotent expansions in Section 2 maintain complete arithmetic purity over the integers, attempting to establish a strictly integer-pure cubic–linear counterexample over the Hermite ring R=ℤR=\mathbb{Z} encounters a fundamental barrier. Although the standard polarization matrix BB inherently introduces fractional coefficients, one can attempt to clear these denominators by scaling the unipotent mapping to the form G⁡(X)=X+6​(Gh−X)G(X)=X+6(G_{h}-X), which successfully forces all matrix entries of BB to lie strictly within ℤ\mathbb{Z}. However, this modification fails to yield an integer-pure Drużkowski reduction because the resulting integral matrix BB loses its right-invertibility over ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

In our 12-dimensional cubic configurations, this obstruction is driven by the fact that the entire cubic part of the second component (Fcub)2(F_{\text{cub}})_{2} is strictly divisible by 12, forcing a factor of 12 into the corresponding minor determinants of BB. Because 12 is not a unit in ℤ\mathbb{Z}, the required right-inverse inevitably introduces fractional coefficients. Interestingly, in our baseline 14-dimensional cubic configuration, the cubic part of (Fcub)2(F_{\text{cub}})_{2} exhibits two terms that form an exception to this uniform divisibility, namely −x1​x2​x11-x_{1}x_{2}x_{11} and −x1​x3​x12-x_{1}x_{3}x_{12}. However, this structural exception does not bypass the underlying ring obstruction; it merely shifts the divisibility by 12 deeper into the network, as the non-linear parts of both baseline auxiliary equations (Fcub)11(F_{\text{cub}})_{11} and (Fcub)12(F_{\text{cub}})_{12} remain strictly divisible by 12. Consequently, the descent to pure Drużkowski linearity inherently breaks the integer purity of the counterexamples, necessitating a transition to the field of rational or complex numbers.

Remark 5.5.

Despite the obstruction preventing the polarization matrix BB from achieving full right-invertibility over the integers, it remains structurally possible to guarantee that the final resulting Drużkowski cubic–linear mapping itself is defined strictly over ℤ\mathbb{Z}. A direct, brute-force approach to clearing the denominators from the construction consists of replacing the finalized Drużkowski map F⁡(Y)F(Y) with the scaled configuration 6−3​F​(63​Y)6^{-3}F(6^{3}Y). Because this substitution uniformly multiplies every non-linear component of the cubic–linear matrix field A​YAY by a factor of 626^{2}, it eliminates any lingering fractional elements and successfully restores the arithmetic integer purity of the polynomial endomorphism.

A more subtle and mathematically elegant alternative exploits the scaling degrees of the extended matrix representations. By selecting the modified unipotent map G⁡(X)=X+6​(Gh−X)G(X)=X+6(G_{h}-X) instead of GhG_{h}, the associated polarization matrix BB becomes a strict matrix over ℤ\mathbb{Z}. Following the parameterizations established in Section 2, the vector (0,t, 0,…, 0, 1)(0,\,t,\,0,\,\dots,\,0,\,1) acts as a parameterized collision point for the deformed mapping X+t−1​(Gh−X)X+t^{-1}(G_{h}-X), with its corresponding preimage coordinates living within the localized ring ℤ⁡[t]\mathbb{Z}[t]. Specializing this locus by substituting t=16t=\frac{1}{6} yields a valid coordinate collision point for the integer-mapped system with preimages defined strictly over the ring of fractions ℤ⁡[16]\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{6}].

Furthermore, since the cubic power xn3x_{n}^{3} is explicitly invoked as a component of the power-linear vector, the final row of the polarization matrix BB simplifies to the standard basis vector eiTe_{i}^{T}. This forcing condition dictates that the ii-th row of the extended matrix CextC_{\text{ext}} takes the form enTe_{n}^{T}, ensuring a direct inverse matching with the extended base C~ext−1=Bext\tilde{C}_{\text{ext}}^{-1}=B_{\text{ext}}. The final Drużkowski transformation maps back to the functional template F⁡(Y)=Y+(A​Bext​Y)×3F(Y)=Y+(AB_{\text{ext}}Y)^{\times 3}. While the first nn rows of BB are defined over ℤ\mathbb{Z}, the remaining m−nm-n columns of CC must span a specific baseline vector space. Because we retain the algebraic freedom to scale these remaining columns of CC arbitrarily, the corresponding reciprocal rows of the inverse matrix BextB_{\text{ext}} scale inversely. Consequently, one can always select a balanced basis scaling such that the complete extended matrix BextB_{\text{ext}} is driven entirely into the integer ring ℤ\mathbb{Z}, achieving a fully integral polynomial mapping over the domain. We have explicitly executed and verified this integral power-linear reduction for our 18-dimensional cubic–homogeneous configuration within the accompanying ancillary file section4d.mac.

However, by exploiting the rich multi-term synergetic profile of our optimal 18-dimensional homogeneous map GhG_{h}, the polarization method drives the system down to an absolute milestone record of exactly 90 variables. The comparative progression of the power-linear reductions across all three evolutionary tracks is systematically summarized below.

The verification matrix ByB_{y} confirms with rank​(By)=90\text{rank}(B_{y})=90 that the cubic mapping expands perfectly into this compressed basis, establishing a historic record-low cubic–linear counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture. The complete automated validation scripts for these systems are preserved across our verification network in section4a.mac, section4b.mac, section4c.mac, and section4d.mac respectively, ensuring immediate numerical reproducibility. In section4d.mac, the stabilization process is tweaked already in the first stage to obtain

H11=2​x1​x9​x19=y1​x1​x18+3​x1​x8​x18H_{11}=2x_{1}x_{9}x_{19}=y_{1}x_{1}x_{18}+3x_{1}x_{8}x_{18}

instead of H11=x1​x9​x19=12​y1​x1​x18+32​x1​x8​x18H_{11}=x_{1}x_{9}x_{19}=\tfrac{1}{2}y_{1}x_{1}x_{18}+\tfrac{3}{2}x_{1}x_{8}x_{18}, to ensure that BB is a matrix over ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

Acknowledgements

The author wishes to express his sincere gratitude to Roy van Rijn and other contributors to Van Rijn’s 12-dimensional cubic counterexample and 19-dimensional cubic-homogeneous counterexample. Prior to learning of his independent numerical results, our stabilization framework had settled at a cubic baseline dimension of 14, homogenizing to dimension 21, and a Drużkowski linearization bound of 123 variables. The insight that a 12-dimensional cubic reduction was structurally achievable served as a powerful catalyst. It inspired the deeper algebraic optimizations detailed in this work, which ultimately allowed us to collapse the system to the current historical records of 12 cubic, 18 cubic-homogeneous, and 90 Drużkowski dimensions.
